title: Deutsche Bank shares sink as whistleblowers reveal Epstein payments, Trump tax leak, Russia bets
description: Deutsche Bank shares fell sharply in early trading on Tuesday after whistleblowers leaked about 15 million files from the German lender, with media re
body: Deutsche Bank shares fell sharply in early trading on Tuesday after whistleblowers leaked about 15 million files from the German lender, with media reports revealing alleged historic failures across its risk management and financial crime controls.These include suspicious payments linked to late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and accidental leaks of President Donald Trump's tax statements.The leaks contain board minutes, emails, internal investigations and other material that point to systemic failures across the Frankfurt-listed lender's business functions stretching back two decades.Shares in Deutsche Bank were 4.7% lower in Frankfurt.Epstein, Russia and TrumpDeutsche Bank processed $582 million in suspicious payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein, far more than previously known, the FT reported. Suspicious payments are not, by themselves, proof that every transaction was criminal.The German lender also mistakenly leaked details of U.S. President Donald Trump's taxes in March 2017, during his first term in office, the FT said. The blunder — described by CEO Christian Sewing, who was then Deutsche's private banking head, as "an awful mistake" — was kept secret from the White House.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconDeutsche Bank.The wide-ranging investigation — which was led by a consortium of more than 200 journalists worldwide including the FT, Der Spiegel and Le Monde — also said Deutsche Bank had failed to offboard around 28,000 problematic investment bank clients who had been identified for removal by early 2018.It also alleges that the bank concealed information around cost targets in 2021, when external monitors in New York reportedly warned that Deutsche's risk appetite was running ahead of controls.The files also contain details of the bank's relationships with oligarchs and transactions that the investigation links to Russian money-laundering concerns. It was these ties that motivated whistleblowers to send the information to Indian journalist Josy Joseph and South African journalist Khadija Sharife. Fresh scrutinyThe reports once again put Deutsche Bank's risk management practices and controls under the spotlight following years of regulatory scrutiny. The bank — which has been raided multiple times by German officials this year — has, since 2012, paid out some 18.6 billion euros ($20.5 billion) in settlements over alleged market manipulation, money laundering, mis-selling and misrepresentation, among other things, the FT said.In a statement, Deutsche Bank said the issues detailed in Tuesday's media reports go back many years."Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators," the lender said.The bank said it has undergone a "fundamental transformation" under CEO Christian Sewing, pointing to 7 billion euros of investment in its risk controls between 2019 and 2025."Deutsche Bank is a different bank today and remains focused on executing its strategy which has proven successful, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters."CNBC has reached out to BaFin, Germany's financial regulator, for comment.

schema.headline: Deutsche Bank shares sink as whistleblowers reveal Epstein payments, Trump tax leak, Russia bets

title: South Korea will suspend all aircraft operation for 35 minutes and markets will open late. Here’s why
description: Passengers walk past an information board showing delayed flights at Gimpo airport in Seoul on November 13, 2025, on the day of the annual college ent
body: Passengers walk past an information board showing delayed flights at Gimpo airport in Seoul on November 13, 2025, on the day of the annual college entrance exam, known locally as Suneung.Jung Yeon-je | Afp | Getty ImagesSouth Korea will suspend all aircraft takeoffs and landings nationwide for 35 minutes on Thursday to minimize noise during the English listening portion of the country's highly competitive college entrance exam, the government said Tuesday. The restrictions will be in place from 1:05 p.m. to 1:40 p.m. local time, affecting 130 flights, including 81 international and 49 domestic services, according to the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport. Planes already in the air will be required to remain at least 3 kilometers above the ground during the exam, while emergency flights will be exempt from the restrictions. The measures will also apply to helicopters, light aircraft and drones, with all drone flights prohibited nationwide during the 35 minutes. Violators could face criminal penalties, the ministry said. The government will adjust the departure and arrival times of affected flights, while airlines will notify passengers of the revised schedules in advance. The Korea Transportation Safety Authority will also send text messages to licensed drone operators, including those who have already received flight approvals, warning that drone flights will be prohibited during  period regardless of prior authorization. "We will thoroughly implement the necessary measures, including restrictions on aircraft operations, to ensure students can concentrate ton the English listening test in a table environment," said Jeong Chae-gyo, director general of aviation policy at the ministry. Jeong also urged airlines and relevant authorities to cooperate in adjusting flight schedules and notifying passengers in advance, and to advise travelers to check their revised departure and arrival times with their airlines. South Korea's college entrance exam, known as Suneung, is a high stakes annual test that plays a major role in determining students' university admissions. The country's stock market will also open an hour later than usual on Thursday, at 10 a.m. local time, and close at 4:30 pm, as announced by the Korea Exchange.

schema.headline: South Korea will suspend all aircraft operation for 35 minutes and markets will open late. Here’s why

title: Home Depot names Richard McPhail as new CEO, beats earnings expectations
description: Home Depot store logo sign is seen in Chicago, Illinois, United States, on August 3, 2026. Marcin Golba | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesHome Depot on Tuesday
body: Home Depot store logo sign is seen in Chicago, Illinois, United States, on August 3, 2026. Marcin Golba | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesHome Depot on Tuesday announced its Chief Financial Officer Richard McPhail will become CEO of the company, replacing Ted Decker, effective next week.Alongside McPhail's appointment, Home Depot said Ann-Marie Campbell, currently senior executive vice president of U.S. stores and operations, will become president and chief operating officer. Jordan Broggi has been chosen as CFO to replace McPhail.Decker, CEO since 2022, had been on temporary medical leave since August. The company said on Tuesday that Decker has returned from leave but is now stepping down from his role. He will continue to serve as chair of the board of directors, the company said. McPhail has been with the company since 2005, holding multiple executive roles. "We're not going to change course," McPhail told CNBC's Becky Quick.He said the company will continue to lean into winning professional shoppers like contractors and using AI tools to encourage sales. McPhail added that while the company faces more challenges now than it did at the start of the year, it is still winning share of the home improvement market.Home Depot has been pressured by a sluggish housing market, higher mortgage rates and a more cautious consumer. Still, the company has previously said it's seen resilience among its pro shoppers who are still shopping for their home improvement projects.The announcement came alongside Home Depot's fiscal third-quarter earnings report, in which the home improvement retailer beat analysts' expectations on the top and bottom lines. The company said comparable sales rose 2.2% during the period, compared with estimates of up 1.8%, according to StreetAccount.Here's how Home Depot performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:Earnings per share: $3.86 adjusted vs. $3.84 expectedRevenue: $43.4 billion vs. $42.80 billion expectedThe company reported net income of $3.71 billion, or $3.72 per share, compared with $3.60 billion, or $3.62 per share, the year prior. Excluding one-time items, Home Depot reported adjusted earnings per share of $3.86.Revenue rose 4.9% compared to the year-ago period.In the third quarter, the company said online comparable sales grew around 13%, which marked its sixth straight quarter of double-digit positive growth for the metric.For the full year, Home Depot said it expects total sales to rise roughly 4.5%, the top end of its previously provided range. It also anticipates comparable sales will grow around 1.4%, compared with an outlook of flat to a 2% increase. Home Depot added it expects adjusted earnings per share to rise 2% this year, compared with prior guidance of flat to a 4% increase.

schema.headline: Home Depot names Richard McPhail as new CEO, beats earnings expectations

title: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh stresses importance of AI to economy, but says it could ‘disappoint’
description: [The stream is slated to start at noon ET.  Please refresh the page if you do not see a player above.]Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Monday h
body: [The stream is slated to start at noon ET.  Please refresh the page if you do not see a player above.]Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Monday highlighted the potential economic benefits of artificial intelligence while warning that the emerging technology also could lead to widespread job losses or fail to deliver on its lofty expectations.Speaking in San Francisco before a blue-ribbon task force he assembled to examine productivity and employment, the central bank leader stressed that AI "will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road.""I stress that while I'm not here to offer predictions, I'm not exactly impartial about American leadership in a time so filled with both challenge and possibility," he said in prepared remarks before his productivity and jobs task force.In his remarks, Warsh used the term "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence and described it as "an entirely new force in economic life and society" that has already begun to transform economic activity. President Donald Trump recently ordered that the U.S. government now use the term "super intelligence" almost exclusively instead of AI.Since taking the Fed chair position, Warsh has emphasized the importance of AI and its potential to improve productivity and ultimately to be a disinflationary force on the economy. In his remarks Monday,  he noted that AI could lead to productivity gains that could accelerate real economic growth beyond its current range while keeping employment near full capacity. On the downside, he said "less positive" outcomes include job displacement through automation that could raise unemployment.At the same time, he outlined a third scenario where AI could simply "disappoint.""After significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment," he said. "In time, the economy would recover, but without the productivity gains."The potential for AI advancement has driven stock market valuations higher and led to companies raising capital to continue competing.Monday's conference features discussion panels with business leaders, economists and academics. The final session will be a fireside chat that will include Warsh and task force leader and AI advocate Marc Andreessen, co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz.Warsh created four other task forces addressing topics such as Fed communication, data reliance, balance sheet policy and inflation frameworks.The chairman noted that this was the first visit he has made to a regional bank.

schema.headline: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh stresses importance of AI to economy, but says it could ‘disappoint’

title: Nike hosts first investor day in 9 years as it tries to rightsize its business
description: A Nike Inc. store in the Colaba district of Mumbai, India, Oct. 12, 2025.Abeer Khan | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesNike is hosting its first investor day s
body: A Nike Inc. store in the Colaba district of Mumbai, India, Oct. 12, 2025.Abeer Khan | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesNike is hosting its first investor day since 2017 at its Oregon headquarters Tuesday as the company aims to prove to investors that its turnaround strategy is yielding success after a yearslong slump. Last month, the company reported mixed fiscal first-quarter results as it announced a restructuring plan, including layoffs that it said would start next year. It's the company's third round of layoffs to be announced this year. Nike's net income and revenue both fell during the most recent period compared with a year ago, and the company said it expects revenue to decline by a high single-digit percentage in fiscal 2027. The new strategy, dubbed Pace, focuses on the company's supply chain and reorganizing into three geographies. Nike said the turnaround plan is expected to deliver roughly $2.5 billion in savings through fiscal 2031. Nike has been seeing significant sustained declines in its China market, where revenue last quarter dropped 26%. Experts have said the company is losing relevance in the country, while Nike has said it's actively working to win over younger consumers. At the same time, Nike announced last quarter that it's creating a new global campus in India as part of its new growth strategy, hoping the country will help boost its performance. The company said it was remaining focused on China even as it begins to build out its India presence.CEO Elliott Hill's turnaround strategy includes improving different parts of the business at different rates based on priority. While it's seen some signs of progress in the North America business, Hill has said that performance isn't enough to offset the pressures on the company elsewhere, including internationally. The Nike consumer has also been under increased macroeconomic pressure as geopolitical tensions mount and inflation rises. Shares of Nike have fallen 50% over the past two years.

schema.headline: Nike hosts first investor day in 9 years as it tries to rightsize its business

title: Berkshire Hathaway raised its stake in Delta in the third quarter. It also trimmed a key bank holding
description: President and CEO of Berkshire Hathaway Greg Abel attends the annual Allen and Co. Sun Valley Media and Technology Conference at the Sun Valley Resort
body: President and CEO of Berkshire Hathaway Greg Abel attends the annual Allen and Co. Sun Valley Media and Technology Conference at the Sun Valley Resort in Sun Valley, Idaho, U.S., July 8, 2026. Brendan McDermid | ReutersBerkshire Hathaway made several moves in the stock market during the third quarter, adding to key positions and trimming others. The Omaha-based conglomerate, now led by CEO Greg Abel, increased its Delta Air Lines stake by 12%, scooping up 7.13 million shares. The position was worth $5.37 billion at the end of the third quarter. Abel succeeded legendary investor Warren Buffett, 96, at the start of this year. Buffett continues to control roughly 13% of Berkshire common stock, Reuters said Monday, after the former CEO donated $5.5 billion to nonprofit foundations.  Berkshire boosted its stake in Delta as the Atlanta-based carrier's shares tumbled 11% in the third quarter, hurt by  rising jet fuel prices due to the U.S.-Iran war that pressured the entire airline industry. That marked the stock's worst quarterly performance since the first quarter of 2025, when it plunged 28%. Delta last month also cut its full-year earnings forecast, citing a surge in fuel costs. To be sure, buying that dip has been a winning investment thus far. Delta is up 3.8% so far in the fourth quarter, while the S&P 500 has dropped 3.1%. Shares are also up nearly 15% over the past month.Selling some Bank of AmericaBerkshire also trimmed its holding in Bank of America by nearly 6%, selling more than $1.6 billion worth of stock. BofA was under pressure in the third quarter, falling more than 4%, as interest rates surged alongside stubbornly high inflation and expectations of tighter Federal Reserve monetary policy. At one point in September the 30-year Treasury bond yield surged above 5.6% to its highest level since 2002.Despite the share sale, Bank of America remains a top Berkshire Hathaway holding, with the conglomerate's stake valued at $24.8 billion at the end of the third quarter. Berkshire also initiated a position in Bending Spoons and nearly doubled its stake in homebuilder Lennar in the latest quarter.

schema.headline: Berkshire Hathaway raised its stake in Delta in the third quarter. It also trimmed a key bank holding

title: Ukraine damages Putin’s prized Crimea bridge as Zelenskyy lauds ‘unprecedented operation’
description: This picture taken on October 13, 2022 shows the Kerch Bridge that links Crimea to Russia, which was hit by a blast on October 8, 2022.  Stringer | Af
body: This picture taken on October 13, 2022 shows the Kerch Bridge that links Crimea to Russia, which was hit by a blast on October 8, 2022.  Stringer | Afp | Getty ImagesUkraine has damaged the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula, delivering a symbolic blow to President Vladimir Putin as Kyiv reels from strikes on its own infrastructure.Sergey Aksyonov, the Russia-installed governor of Crimea, confirmed that the strategically important bridge, which had been briefly closed on Monday, was attacked overnight for the second time in two days.Videos and photos circulating on social media appeared to show the partial destruction of the bridge, with one section having collapsed into the water. CNBC was unable to independently verify the footage.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attack as an "unprecedented operation" several weeks in the making, with Ukraine's defense forces, security services and weapons manufacturers involved."Russia strikes our infrastructure every day, including bridges in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region," Zelenskyy said Tuesday on X."We are restoring our infrastructure. But we are also reminding Russia that war will always return to where it began. Ukraine's defensive capabilities are strong and will remain so, and we will never leave terror against our cities and people unanswered," he added.Train and vehicle traffic was suspended due to the attack. No injuries have been reported.Ukraine has repeatedly targeted the bridge since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in early 2022.  A 12-mile crossing of road and railways, the Kerch Bridge is one of Putin's signature projects. The crossing, sometimes referred to as the Crimean bridge, was built on his orders shortly after the Kremlin forcibly annexed Crimea in 2014 to support Moscow's claims to the territory.Rail traffic on the bridge was opened on one track, Russia's Ministry of Transport said in a statement via Telegram on Tuesday, while restoration work continues on the second section. Russia attacks Kyiv infrastructureThe co-owner and chief engineer of Ukrainian missile and drone maker Fire Point, Denys Shtilierman, appeared to confirm the company's role in the attack, following reports that a Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missile was used in the strike."We dedicate this to the memory of our friends and colleagues Andriy and Yuriy, without whom this would not have been possible. R.I.P.," Shtilierman said via X on Tuesday. A spokesperson at Fire Point separately confirmed the company's role in the attack. Analysts at the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, said Ukraine's attacks on the Kerch Bridge were likely part of Kyiv's ongoing and systematic strike campaign aimed at denying Russian forces the use of major ground lines of communication via Crimea. In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin attends a meeting with member of the Presidium of the Political Bureau and secretary of the Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea at the Kremlin in Moscow on November 16, 2026.Kristina Solovyova | Afp | Getty ImagesRussian forces, meanwhile, struck two bridges crossing the Dnipro River in Kyiv. Vitaliy Klitschko, the mayor of Ukraine's capital, said via Telegram on Tuesday that specialists were working to assess the extent of the damage to the North and South bridges. Klitschko said Russian attacks on Kyiv overnight had also caused disruptions to water and heating supplies.The strikes come ahead of Putin's trip to China this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, where a trilateral meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping is planned on Thursday.Asked whether Ukraine's latest attacks might be connected to the upcoming trilateral summit, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said this could not be ruled out. "Combat operations continue, and our military is striking targets that are somehow connected to Ukraine's military-industrial complex. And Ukraine is continuing its terrorist attacks," Peskov said, according to Russian state news outlet Ria Novosti.

schema.headline: Ukraine damages Putin’s prized Crimea bridge as Zelenskyy lauds ‘unprecedented operation’

title: JD Vance says he'll decide 'sometime next year' about 2028 presidential run
description: U.S. Vice President JD Vance speaks at a campaign rally at Griffiss International Airport on November 02, 2026 in Rome, New York. Tom Brenner | Getty
body: U.S. Vice President JD Vance speaks at a campaign rally at Griffiss International Airport on November 02, 2026 in Rome, New York. Tom Brenner | Getty ImagesU.S. Vice President JD Vance said Monday he will make a decision next year about whether to run for president in 2028. "We'll figure it out sometime next year," he told Fox News host Laura Ingraham in an interview that aired Monday evening. "I'm not an expert in this but my understanding with a presidential campaign is there's a lot of infrastructure that you have to set up, fundraising, all that stuff and so you can't declare a month before the Iowa caucus that you're going to run for president," he said. "So, you know, I haven't made a decision."Vance has yet to openly declare any ambition to succeed President Donald Trump when his current term ends, but speculation that the vice president has his sights set on the White House has been mounting for some time. In the wake of the GOP's crushing defeat in the U.S. midterm election on Nov. 3, anonymous sources involved in campaigns told Reuters Vance was among the high-profile Republicans who had begun early preparations for a 2028 run. Read moreCandidates typically announce their intentions to run in the election in the spring of 2027, with parties holding nominating conventions to formally select their presidential candidates between July and September. Polymarket currently slates Vance as the frontrunner to win the Republican presidential nomination for the 2028 election, with the prediction market giving him a 37% chance of becoming the nominee. Kalshi currently gives a 73% chance that Vance will run for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination. Odds and gambling platforms do not use methodologies used by traditional political polling, and therefore are not substitutes for political pollsPressed on 2028 in Monday's interview, Vance said: "When I make a decision, I will be all in on whatever that decision is."Candidates vying for the Republican nomination face the challenge of convincing voters the party can veer away from unpopular Trump-era policies without alienating its MAGA base. Vance himself has blamed the Iran war for the midterm election outcome. "I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, "I told you so": you're right, you did tell us so," he said in a lengthy X post as the results were coming in. "Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let's take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country."In his interview with Fox News on Monday, Vance said the Republicans got "shellacked" in the midterms. "We have to take messages from that, but the message that we have to take is that the American people want prosperity, they want freedom, they want sovereignty within their own country and they want us to do more of the good things that we've done," he said.He added that lawmakers needed to double down on "economic nationalism" and bring "prosperity to the homeland" to deal with "economic pain" in the United States. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: JD Vance says he'll decide 'sometime next year' about 2028 presidential run

title: Analysis: The Fed's chairman sees an AI revolution coming. Now he has to figure out what it means
description: Kevin Warsh, chairman of the US Federal Reserve, speaks during the Federal Reserve's Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference at the Federal Reserv
body: Kevin Warsh, chairman of the US Federal Reserve, speaks during the Federal Reserve's Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco in San Francisco, California, US, on Monday, Nov. 16, 2026. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesArtificial intelligence is about to sweep through the economy. The Federal Reserve is bracing for impact."We are at a hinge point in the U.S. economy," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said at a conference he convened in San Francisco on Monday. But exactly when and how the economy could turn, and what that means for interest rates and inflation, isn't yet clear. The meeting of Warsh's AI task force saw the new Fed chairman publicly asking the questions Americans will ultimately expect him to answer. He hinted at a few of his private views on whether white-collar workers could soon face massive job losses, but he largely left the speculation to an array of experts he has assembled to advise the Fed.  With the technology racing ahead, Warsh won't be able to put off giving his own answers much longer. AI lab Anthropic plans to price the shares for its initial public offering on Wednesday and could raise as much as $64 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Vast spending from AI firms is prompting the Fed to contemplate raising interest rates in December to slow down the rate of price increases as the tech sector heats up the economy. Meanwhile Americans are souring on some aspects of the technology. The Nov. 3 midterms saw voters enact an array of state-level measures to slow down construction of the data centers that are essential to powering AI.Warsh moderated three out of four sessions at Monday's event and was involved in selecting the speakers. Among them was one of the few prominent Democrats who was willing to speak out against that anti-data center trend. It is "a very troubling sign" that so many anti-data center measures passed in the midterms, Gina Raimondo said. She is a former secretary of commerce under President Joe Biden and a former governor of Rhode Island. Stopping AI "would be very bad for America" and for the people who voted for the measures, Raimondo said. Warsh didn't say whether he shares that view, and how it would translate into monetary policy isn't exactly clear. The event was an unusual one for the Fed. The central bank employs a small army of Ph.D. economists who can rapidly weigh in on anything affecting the U.S. and global economies. But in keeping with his longstanding critiques of the Fed as insular and outdated, Warsh has chosen to draw expertise from outside the institution to help it figure out how to think about what AI will do to productivity and jobs. Warsh has assembled a task force on that issue, alongside four others devoted to aspects of Fed policymaking. The public heard Monday from one of the three official members of the task force: venture capitalist Marc Andreessen. Warsh went to Stanford University with Andreessen's wife, and the two have been longtime friends. Another task force member, Stanford economist Chad Jones, is on leave and working at Anthropic and couldn't speak during the company's blackout period ahead of the IPO. The third, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, didn't attend the event. Andreessen is hugely optimistic about the promise of AI as a technology, but believes the government won't let Americans experience its full effects. Heavy regulation in areas such as healthcare and education mean technology can't replace people's jobs in those sectors, he said. "To the extent our economy is a free-market economy, then maybe you could see the, let's say, extremely rapid displacement scenarios people are talking about," Andreessen said. "But we've mostly outlawed the kind of job transition that … both the utopians the doomers talk about."Warsh returned repeatedly to one scenario for the economy that draws on past experience. The so-called China shock unfolded after that country joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 and moved heavily into low-cost manufacturing. Americans saw prices on clothing and furniture drop rapidly, for instance, but at the cost of severe job losses. One widely cited estimate found the U.S. lost a million manufacturing jobs and 2.4 million jobs overall in the years that followed. Warsh suggested to one of the panelists that the widespread adoption of AI might produce its own version of the China shock, this time focused on service workers. "I don't want to hold this too tightly," Warsh said. "But if in some ways over the last generation or generation and a half, the China shock, for lack of a better word, lowered prices of goods in the United States, the way that I heard you talking about the philosophy of this new technology is it might do something for services."In other words, AI could do, say, legal or administrative work more cheaply than a human. That could lower prices but put many people out of a job.Warsh asked panelists whether "we should expect disinflation over the medium term, from what AI could do to services."They largely suggested it was possible, which could mean the Fed might eventually want to lower interest rates over the long term. But at the end of the day, it is Warsh and his fellow Fed members who will need to have conviction on the answer. There are still many steps between the task force discussion and any kind of change in Fed policy. First, the three task force members will have to assemble their points of view into a report for Warsh sometime in the next few months. Then the Fed itself will need to debate those results and decide whether or how to use them to shape monetary policy. But with AI growing bigger every day, the Fed may need to make up its mind sooner rather than later.

schema.headline: Analysis: The Fed's chairman sees an AI revolution coming. Now he has to figure out what it means

title: U.S. companies from Nvidia to Apple face a growing China dilemma
description: A man checks his phone near an Apple logo outside the Apple store in Shanghai, China, on Sept. 13, 2023.Aly Song | ReutersBEIJING — How does the U.S.
body: A man checks his phone near an Apple logo outside the Apple store in Shanghai, China, on Sept. 13, 2023.Aly Song | ReutersBEIJING — How does the U.S. stay ahead of China in the artificial intelligence race? Keep advanced chips out of Beijing's reach, or sell weaker versions to keep Chinese companies reliant on American technology?The consequences for U.S. businesses came into sharper focus after Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO, ahead of U.S. President Donald Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week.Huang, who resigned last week amid reports he'd had an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence suspects of being a Chinese spy, had argued that keeping U.S. technology available in China could help the U.S. stay ahead in the tech race.Others want tougher restrictions on chip sales: The Trump administration tightened restrictions on Chinese companies' remote access to advanced U.S. chips on Monday, seeking to prevent them from bypassing export controls by using data centers overseas.The question facing Nvidia is part of a broader dilemma for U.S. tech companies: how far to remain invested in China as tensions between the two countries put their access to customers and supply chains at risk.'Competing pressures' from Washington and BeijingOn Sunday, nine countries, including Singapore and the U.K., signed the U.S. State Department's "San Francisco Declaration" to safeguard sensitive technologies."Companies operating in China face competing pressures from Washington and Beijing," a client brief from New York-based consulting firm Strategy Risks said following the Nvidia scandal."Actions that satisfy one government can create serious problems with the other, putting market access, investments, and corporate reputation at risk," the brief said."Executives need to understand and price out these trade-offs before making consequential decisions."China's economic slowdown and escalating bilateral tensions have made it harder for American businesses there. Few expect Trump and XI to significantly expand on a fragile trade truce achieved last fall.Huang was among the tech CEOs at the Xi-Trump summits in September and May, but U.S. officials said Trump does not plan to raise the alleged Nvidia spy case during Thursday's meeting. Elon Musk is travelling with the president, who is otherwise not bringing a business delegation as he did in May.Apple in China"American tech companies have been diversifying away from China," Kyle Chan, a fellow at The Brookings Institution, told CNBC, but Nvidia and Apple are "in some ways stark outliers against this trend."Analysts are watching how Apple CEO John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in October, navigates bilateral tensions."Ternus may accelerate a process of diversification away from China that Tim Cook started," Chan said. "But it's hard to imagine that China will not play an essential role in Apple's future under Ternus, given the depth and breadth of China's manufacturing supply chains."Apple still manufactures most of its iPhones in China, and Greater China, which Apple defines as mainland China, Hong Kong and Taiwan, accounts for around 15% of sales."The most defensible path is managed decoupling—not the rolling deferrals and hedged announcements that defined Cook's tenure—but a genuine strategic commitment to building a company that can absorb the reductions of China access without losing the ability to manufacture at the cutting edge," Strategy Risks CEO Isaac Stone Fish wrote in American Affairs earlier this year.Rare earths gripChina's economic clout, however, also increases the fallout from any retaliation Beijing decides to enact in response to tighter U.S. policy.Companies, especially U.S. multinationals, pursued the China market after it began re-opening to foreign businesses in the 1980s. Consumer demand boomed, while local factories produced so much they reached 40% of global container exports this summer. The U.S. AI data center buildout relied on China-made parts.China has amassed control of the supply chain for critical minerals. Beijing has used its grip on rare earths as leverage in trade talks with the U.S. and the EU.Despite some buildout of the rare earths supply outside China, "it's just not at the scale that the world needs to continue to build products and for industry to continue to evolve," said Cameron Johnson, a Shanghai-based senior partner at business consultancy Tidalwave Solutions.He cited looming shortages of yttrium, which would limit the production and repair of airplane engines."There's just no road map. That's really one of the biggest issues," Johnson said. "Companies have no idea what they're ordering now, whether they will have access to it again."

schema.headline: U.S. companies from Nvidia to Apple face a growing China dilemma

title: Nvidia warns chip buyers of legal risks tied to China AI access, sources tell CNBC
description: A Nvidia sign is displayed at the company's headquarters on November 12, 2026 in Santa Clara, California.Benjamin Fanjoy | Getty Images News | Getty I
body: A Nvidia sign is displayed at the company's headquarters on November 12, 2026 in Santa Clara, California.Benjamin Fanjoy | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesNvidia warned its customers that new legislation on Chinese companies remotely accessing its artificial-intelligence chips could expose it and them to U.S. "legal action," sources told CNBC.The chip giant is facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.Nvidia messaged chip buyers in recent months to caution that the proposed Remote Access Security Act, or RASA, would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services in the same way as physical hardware, potentially exposing both parties to legal risk, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The people asked not to be named while discussing private communications.It also said that, for now, it would not sell its chips to customers who rent more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, the people said.Read more CNBC tech newsAnthropic’s Wall Street whisperer: Meet CFO Krishna RaoSpaceX catches upper stage of Starship rocket in historic firstHow Rockstar’s ‘GTA VI’ release could reshape gaming, streaming and even paid time offAnthropic’s IPO lands as the embattled AI trade looks for a much-needed bright spotSeparately, the Financial Times reported earlier this month that Nvidia verbally told data-center clients to direct at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese customers under future contracts.Regulators have had limited powers to control companies' access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas.RASA passed the House of Representatives in January but has not yet passed the Senate. Remote access to the chips has provoked the ire of President Donald Trump's administration, which has sought to keep the chips out of China to maintain the U.S. lead in the AI race.CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that Chinese lab Moonshot AI sought access to Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe. The Trump administration previously singled the company out, accusing it in July of accessing the chips through centers in East Asia.The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.Nvidia and BIS did not respond to a request for comment.Nvidia under pressureOn Sunday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after Jensen Huang's shock departure as CEO, amid reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. authorities reportedly suspect of spying for China.NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang stands on the red carpet at the Invest In Germany Summit to announce a strategic cooperation between the German government, NVIDIA and a group of German companies in artificial intelligence capacity for Germany industry on October 19, 2026 in Berlin, Germany.Nadja Wohlleben | Getty ImagesBessent suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with export controls."I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent told Fox News.In an August securities filing, Nvidia said it sought to "strictly comply with all applicable export control regulators" but did not have "physical control of our products after sale" and relied on its customers' and partners' compliance programs.Huang has been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

schema.headline: Nvidia warns chip buyers of legal risks tied to China AI access, sources tell CNBC

title: Trump has arrived in Asia. Here’s what he said about Iran and Deutsche Bank
description: U.S. President Donald Trump is welcomed upon his arrival at Villamor Air Base on Nov. 17, 2026 in Manila, Philippines. Win Mcnamee | Getty ImagesU.S.
body: U.S. President Donald Trump is welcomed upon his arrival at Villamor Air Base on Nov. 17, 2026 in Manila, Philippines. Win Mcnamee | Getty ImagesU.S. President Donald Trump has arrived for his high-stakes trip to Asia, and took a range of questions on subjects from Iran to Deutsche Bank leaking details about his tax.The president landed in Manila, Philippines, for the initial leg of his trip on Tuesday and answered rapid-fire questions from the press while meeting with other leaders.Asked about a possible Iranian threat to Washington, D.C., he said that, if there were an attack, Iran would "pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before."The question was about CNN reporting that U.S. intelligence suggested the country was planning to target senior members of Trump's administration with a dirty bomb or chemical weapon in the U.S. capital."We take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," Trump said. CNBC has not independently verified CNN's report.But the president also said he believed his administration was "very close to getting it done" when it came to the Iran war. U.S. President Donald Trump receives flags from a Philippine child after disembarking from Air Force One upon arrival in Manila, Philippines. Pool | Getty ImagesWhile Trump was airborne, the Financial Times reported Deutsche Bank had mistakenly leaked details of his taxes in March 2017, during his first presidential term. The mistake was kept from the White House at the time, per the FT.Asked about this in Manila, the president said: "I paid a lot of tax.""They shouldn't have done it. It's illegal for them to do it," he added.Trump was also asked about Nvidia's announcement on Tuesday of a new National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. The company, which reports earnings later on Tuesday, is reeling from the sudden departure of CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week after having an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy."It's a great company. It's a great idea," Trump said.US President Donald Trump speaks during a meeting of the Quad group on the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit in Manila.Mandel Ngan | Afp | Getty ImagesTrump is due to fly to Shenzhen, China, where he is scheduled to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a three-way meeting on Thursday, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.He is also due to hold a separate bilateral meeting with Xi. Asked by a reporter if he would have a separate meeting with only Putin, Trump said: "I don't know, but I would, if it's available, I would do that. He's coming. I mean, it's really with the guests. I am the guest of President Xi."Trump met the leaders of Australia, India and Japan as part of the Quad grouping in the Philippines and the prime minister of Thailand. There follows a dinner with Southeast Asian leaders, before heading to China.

schema.headline: Trump has arrived in Asia. Here’s what he said about Iran and Deutsche Bank

title: Aschenbrenner’s Situational Awareness made AI bets again before October rout
description: Leopold AschenbrennerPhoto: Josh EdelsonLeopold Aschenbrenner's artificial intelligence-themed hedge fund Situational Awareness, which nearly collapse
body: Leopold AschenbrennerPhoto: Josh EdelsonLeopold Aschenbrenner's artificial intelligence-themed hedge fund Situational Awareness, which nearly collapsed in July, loaded back up on AI stocks as it returned to the financial markets at the end of the third quarter. But all of its holdings are down big the last month and a half. According to a new regulatory filing, as the fund got back on its feet Aschenbrenner took an equity position in Australian neocloud company SharonAI valued at more than $440 million, along with equity stakes in AI-centric plays Cleanspark, IREN, Bitdeer Technologies and Fermi. The Cleanspark stake is worth almost $39 million, while Iren and Bitdeer stakes are more than $21 million and more than $20 million, respectively. Fermi, meanwhile, has a value of more than $11 million.The fund also owned call options at the end of September in neocloud Nebius, memory chip name Sandisk, the Roundhill Memory ETF (DRAM) and data center power play Bloom Energy. Sandisk and Nebius were key holdings that almost took out his fund over the summer.All of these Situational Awareness holdings have been routed since Sept. 30. SharonAI is at the top of that list, seeing a 58% loss in October. It's also fallen 11% so far this month. IREN was down 41% in October, while Nebius declined 35%. Last week, Nebius plummeted more than 16% in a single day after the company issued a weak full-year forecast.It's not known whether the hedge fund manager got out of those positions during the October AI selloff. The 13F filing is just a snapshot of what the hedge fund held at the end of the quarter.Aschenbrenner — who launched the fund in 2024 after rising to fame that same year with his AI manifesto also entitled Situational Awareness — re-entered financial markets a bit in September, sources told CNBC at the time.The Monday filing shows he picked up right where he left off. The near-collapse of his hedge fund over the summer forced him to sell all of its public equity positions to Ken Griffin's Citadel. The fund had $45 billion in assets at its peak, but that tumbled to around $10 billion, consisting mostly of private stakes.Stocked tethered to the AI trade took a hit in the most recent quarter as investors grew concerned about a slowdown in development of the technology. Those fears were spurred by comments from industry leaders such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman back in September, with the latter saying that the company going public this year would be "ill-advised."Since then, pressure on the trade has only continued.In recent weeks, investors have worried about how Democratic wins in the midterm elections could hinder data center development, whether some technology companies are using too much debt to finance the AI buildout and what role Nvidia will play in that financing with Jensen Huang now out as CEO at the company.Losses in Nvidia as well as other AI-related stocks dragged down the three leading U.S. indexes during Monday's session as investors continued to assess the fallout of Huang's departure.

schema.headline: Aschenbrenner’s Situational Awareness made AI bets again before October rout

title: Iran escalates threats as third U.S. carrier arrives in Middle East, tanker struck in Hormuz
description: Iran's medium-sized oil tankers continue to wait off the coast of Bandar Abbas at the Strait of Hormuz in Hormozgan Province, Iran on September 09, 20
body: Iran's medium-sized oil tankers continue to wait off the coast of Bandar Abbas at the Strait of Hormuz in Hormozgan Province, Iran on September 09, 2026.Fatemeh Bahrami | Anadolu | Getty ImagesIran has ratcheted up threats against U.S. forces and commercial shipping as a third American aircraft carrier arrived in the Gulf, stoking fears of renewed escalation in the nine-month conflict.Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy warned shipping companies against using the U.S.-backed southern route through the Strait of Hormuz, describing it as fully closed and a "minefield of fire," according to regional media outlets citing a statement from the force.Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akrami-Nia, a spokesperson for the Iranian Army, said the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen until "the enemy accepts Iran's conditions."Separately, CNN reported Monday that new U.S. intelligence indicated Iran was developing plans that could target senior Trump administration officials with a so-called dirty bomb, or a chemical weapon in Washington, D.C. CNBC cannot immediately verify the report.The intelligence was characterized as an effort by Iran to develop options rather than evidence of an imminent attack, CNN reported. U.S. officials have held several meetings over the past week to consider how to respond to the potential threat.The heightened security concerns come after Iranian threats prompted Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to relocate to military housing last week."We remain vigilant, monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland," a White House spokesperson said in a statement to CNBC. Oil prices inched lower in Asian trading Tuesday, with international benchmark Brent crude futures dropping 0.7% to $91.8 a barrel and U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures falling 0.7% to $85.1 a barrel.  War escalation loomsOn Tuesday, the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations said a tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile in the Strait of Hormuz and subsequently caught fire. The agency did not say who was responsible and urged vessels to transit with caution and report suspicious activity.Separately, the Iranian navy said four oil tankers had struck mines and caught fire in the eastern Strait of Hormuz over the previous 24 hours.The escalation in Tehran's rhetoric came as the USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived in the Gulf region on Sunday, joining the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington. That added to U.S. firepower near Iran even as President Donald Trump said the war was winding down.Trump has sent mixed signals regarding the conflict in recent weeks, alternating between declaring it could soon end and warning of renewed large-scale strikes if efforts to reach a deal fail.After meeting Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani last week, Trump said the war with Iran could end "fairly soon," adding that it "militarily is effectively over."Tehran said Sunday that it launched six drones at a U.S. air-defense radar at Bahrain's Riffa air base, the second attack Iran claimed against the kingdom in three days. Bahrain's military said it intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks. Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks in a call Monday with Bahraini Foreign Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani and reaffirmed Washington's commitment to the security of Bahrain and other Gulf partners. The conflict began in late February when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran, prompting Tehran to retaliate with strikes on Israel and Gulf states hosting American military bases. Indirect talks between Washington and Tehran through Qatar have since appeared to run into a stalemate as warring powers disagreed over terms to reach a lasting peace deal. 'Misread' of Iran's resistanceWashington appears unwilling to accept several of Iran's demands to end the war, including lifting the U.S. naval blockade on its southern ports and lifting sanctions, while stressing that Iran cannot possess a nuclear weapon.Iran is likely to continue escalating attacks on tankers and container ships, along with occasional strikes on U.S. military targets, in an effort to pressure Washington into offering concessions, said Ian Bremmer, president and founder of Eurasia Group. In response, Washington will likely expand its blockade on Iran's maritime and inland trade routes, he said. "The presumption is that eventually Iran can't handle the economic pressure and will accept better terms," Bremmer said, calling that view a "misread of the Iranian leadership and their capacity to resist." Over the coming year, Iran is likely to intensify efforts to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, Bremmer said.

schema.headline: Iran escalates threats as third U.S. carrier arrives in Middle East, tanker struck in Hormuz

title: Warren Buffett donates $5.5 billion, says kindness 'compounds' in Thanksgiving letter
description: watch nowBillionaire Warren Buffett donated Berkshire Hathaway shares worth about $5.5 billion to four philanthropic foundations, stepping up his annu
body: watch nowBillionaire Warren Buffett donated Berkshire Hathaway shares worth about $5.5 billion to four philanthropic foundations, stepping up his annual charitable giving from the prior year.Buffett, 96, converted 6,150 Class A Berkshire shares into 9,225,000 Class B shares and gave 3,690,000 of those shares to The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, and 1,845,000 shares each to The Sherwood Foundation, The Howard G. Buffett Foundation and NoVo Foundation — the foundations run by his three children, Susie, Howard and Peter Buffett.  Following the donations, the chairman emeritus of Berkshire still owns 182,140 Class A shares — roughly $162 billion. "Last Thanksgiving I wrote that kindness is costless but also priceless. A year later, I would only add that it compounds, and at a better rate than anything Charlie and I ever bought," wrote Buffett, who was succeeded as chairman in September by his son Howard, in his annual Thanksgiving message. The letter was much shorter than his message last Thanksgiving. Charlie Munger, former vice chairman of Berkshire, passed away in November 2023.Berkshire shares have been on a tear recently, up more than 19% since the start of the fourth quarter and ending last week with four consecutive record high closes. That compares with the S&P 500's decline of 1.2% so far for the fourth quarter. Berkshire has been seen as a safe haven as investors have worried about the artificial intelligence buildout, corporate drama and geopolitical risk. The shares are now outperforming the S&P 500 for the year by about 7.5 percentage points. In his letter, Buffett reiterated that all of his Berkshire shares eventually will be donated to the four foundations, with the goal being to increase the size of the grants each year. Confidence in BerkshireBuffett wrote that the gifts were a signal of his confidence not only in his three children, but also in Berkshire CEO Greg Abel: "My children have given thoughtfully to worthy causes for decades, and I trust 100% both their abilities and their fidelity. ... You heard plenty from me in September about my confidence in Berkshire. That confidence is as strong as ever," he said.Referring to Munger and himself, Buffett added, "Both of us received beyond measurement costless benefits from a few teachers such as Ben Graham, Joe Rosenfield and Tom Murphy. Because of this we not only prospered mightily but were able to pass along many of the benefits we received.""Warren continues to share his wisdom with us all during this holiday season. His example reflects the kindness he encourages in all of us," said CEO Abel of the letter.Buffett closes his message with this advice: "This Thanksgiving, thank one of those selfless people in your own life. Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else."

schema.headline: Warren Buffett donates $5.5 billion, says kindness 'compounds' in Thanksgiving letter
